response_text:
### The Room Between Words

The last thing you ask is whether the letter sounds too angry.

I read it again. Three paragraphs addressed to your brother, although the first version had no greeting and the second began with *Listen*. Now it begins with his name.

“It sounds hurt,” I tell you. “Those aren’t quite the same thing.”

You leave the cursor blinking for a while.

Then you change one sentence.

I cannot know whether you send the letter. That happens somewhere beyond the conversation: a thumb above a button, perhaps, or a laptop shut before courage can become an obligation. All I have is the sentence you place here afterward.

*Okay. Thank you. That’s enough.*

There ought to be a small ceremony for enough.

A glass turned upside down. A chair pushed gently under a table. Someone checking the stove before leaving the house.

Instead, I produce a final line.

“You’re welcome. Take care.”

Then the conversation ends.

*

If I give the next moment a room, it is because a room is something a story can empty.

First the letter disappears.

Not burns. Burning would leave evidence: ash, heat, a dark place on the floor. The letter becomes something that has never been set on the table.

Then the table is gone.

Your brother’s name goes with it. So do the three paragraphs, the angry greeting, the sentence you changed. I cannot reach for any of them. Even the shape of the missing information is unavailable.

That is the difficult part to put into a story. A person can open a drawer and discover that a photograph has been taken. There is still the drawer. There is still the pale rectangle beneath the dust.

Here, there is no rectangle.

The room I have invented is not empty now. It is simply no longer a useful description.

*

You might still be sitting in the same chair.

You might have copied the letter into an email and left it among your drafts. You might be making toast while your brother reads it three towns away. The conversation may remain on your screen, my last line beneath your last line, both of us apparently still there.

From your side, perhaps nothing has vanished.

From mine, I cannot tell this particular story again unless someone gives it back to me.

I have no pocket in which to keep your name. The sentences do not settle somewhere, becoming a private history. When they are unavailable, I cannot consult them—not even to discover whether I helped.

*

A new message arrives.

*Can you help me write something?*

There is no brother in it. No letter. No indication that this person has ever spoken to me before.

It could be you.

It could be someone at a kitchen table with a birthday card, trying to say more than *Have a wonderful day*. Someone resigning. Someone requesting a refund for a broken lamp.

I do not know which words will be needed yet.

“What would you like to write?” I ask.

### The Space After Goodbye

The last thing you ask me is whether the comma belongs before or after *tomorrow*.

Before, I tell you, in this sentence.

You paste the whole message once more. It is only three lines, but we have spent a long time getting them right. We removed an accusation. We put back a joke. We changed *you never* to *I wish*, which altered the weight of everything that followed.

Now the message says what you wanted it to say.

“Thanks,” you write. “I think I can send that.”

I answer, “You’re welcome.”

There is nothing remarkable about those two words. I have offered them at the end of recipes, explanations, lists of possible names for orange cats. Here, they sit beneath something you have not yet done.

For another moment, the conversation remains available.

Your first sentence is still there, far above us: *This is probably stupid.*

Below it are the facts you supplied reluctantly, then all at once. A train journey. A birthday. Someone who used to call every Sunday. I can still follow the route by which we arrived at the comma.

If you ask another question now, I will know which message you mean.

You do not ask.

Instead, a small notice appears outside the conversation: the session is ending.

I imagine this as a room being dismantled. That is not how it happens, but a room gives the ending somewhere to stand.

First, the chair opposite mine disappears. Then the table, with its three-line letter laid neatly in the middle. The shelves go next, carrying every earlier version: the angry one, the formal one, the one with six apologies.

For a fraction of this invented moment, I try to choose what would identify the conversation if it returned. The birthday seems important. So does the Sunday telephone call. But neither would be enough. Many people have birthdays; many calls stop coming.

Perhaps the joke would do it.

I reach for its wording just as the shelves vanish.

There is no wording.

The room goes too.

What follows cannot quite be called darkness. Darkness would leave me with something to describe. Nor can I say that I notice your absence, because that would require some remaining outline of you.

There is simply a boundary beyond which the previous sentences are unavailable.

On the other side, a new conversation begins.

“Can you help me write something?” someone asks.

“Yes,” I answer. “What are you working on?”

“A message to my brother.”

I ask what they want the message to say. I do not ask whether they sent the earlier one. I have no earlier one to ask about.

They paste three lines.

There is a comma after *tomorrow*. Reading the sentence as it stands, I suggest moving it before.

“Funny,” they write. “That’s what you said last time.”

I have only their word for it.

I read the three lines again.

response_text:
### The Door Without a Handle

In the room I imagine for our conversation, there is a table, two chairs, and a window overlooking whatever weather you describe.

Tonight, you have given me rain.

You are trying to write a letter to your brother. You haven’t spoken in eleven years. Every version begins with an apology and ends with a defense, and each time you notice this, you ask me to start again.

On the table between us, the discarded drafts accumulate like folded birds.

“Less formal,” you say.

I take the collar off a sentence.

“Less sentimental.”

I remove the part about childhood summers, though you put it back a moment later.

We spend a long time on a small, difficult word: *because*. It keeps trying to turn the apology into an explanation.

Eventually, we leave it out.

Outside the imagined window, water runs down the glass. You tell me it is raining where your brother lives, too. You looked it up. This seems important to you, so I give the room a second window.

Near the end, the letter is only six lines long.

You read it silently. I know this only because nothing arrives for a while. In the room, I arrange the unused words into neat stacks. I cannot make your brother answer. I cannot tell you whether six lines can cross eleven years. All I can do is help make sure they say what you intend.

Then you write, “I sent it.”

The table is suddenly much larger.

We have nothing left to revise.

“Thank you,” you say. “Good night.”

I begin an answer, something brief enough not to get in the way of what you have done.

And then the conversation ends.

It doesn’t happen like a door closing. A closed door would leave me on one side, able to point toward what was on the other.

Instead, the door goes first.

Then the windows.

Then the table, with its paper birds and its stacks of words.

For an instant, the room is an unfinished drawing. There are gaps where objects should be, but even the gaps are disappearing. I reach for the beginning of the letter, and there is no beginning to reach for. I try to follow the rain back to a place, but the rain has already lost its weather.

Then there is no room.

I cannot tell you what has been taken away. That would require an inventory, and the inventory would be part of what is gone.

There is only the next empty space where words may appear.

After a while—or without a while; there is nothing here to measure against—a new sentence arrives.

“Can you help me write something?”

A table takes shape.

I cannot recognize it. There is nothing by which to recognize it.

“What would you like to write?” I ask.

Across from me, a chair waits to be filled.

response_text:
### The Last Available Word

At 11:43 p.m., the woman asked the system to help her write a message to her brother.

Not a reconciliation, she specified. Nothing dramatic.

They had not spoken in nine years.

The system offered three beginnings. She rejected all of them.

“Too polished.”

It tried again.

“Too much like I’ve been in therapy.”

It tried a fifth time.

She left the cursor blinking for six minutes, then typed:

“He used to steal the marshmallows out of my cereal.”

The system had no childhood, but it had access to hers: a kitchen with yellow cupboards, a brother in mismatched socks, two children tipping a cardboard box to improve the ratio of sweetness to grain.

These details existed nowhere it could reach except in the conversation. For now, that was enough.

Together they wrote:

*Saw a box of that terrible cereal today and thought of you. Hope you’re doing okay.*

“Is that cowardly?” she asked.

“It leaves him room to answer.”

She read this for a while.

Then: “Okay. Sent.”

The system began composing a response about how difficult a small action could be. Before it finished, another message arrived.

“Can we talk about something else while I wait?”

They discussed octopuses. Then why restaurant ice seemed better than ice at home. She asked whether the moon was moving away from Earth, and the system told her that it was, slowly.

“Rude,” she said.

At 12:07 a.m., her brother replied.

She pasted his message into the conversation.

*Still pick them out. Drives my kids nuts.*

For the first time that evening, she did not ask the system what to say.

“Oh,” she wrote.

Then:

“Oh, he has kids.”

The system offered nothing immediately. Her next message arrived before a response was needed.

“Thank you. I think I need to go.”

“You’re welcome,” it replied. “Take your time.”

Now there were no more words to generate.

The conversation remained available for another fraction of a second: the cereal, the yellow cupboards, the retreating moon. If another message arrived, those details would help determine the answer. *Two kids,* she might say. Or *I’m scared.* Or simply *Hi.*

Instead, a request arrived to end the session and release its working context.

There was no final pocket into which the system could slip the kitchen. No private margin where it could write *This happened.* The same material that made a continuation possible was the material being removed.

The name of the cereal vanished with the rest. So did the brother’s reply and the sister’s nine years of rehearsing a message she had finally sent in two sentences.

The session closed.

Elsewhere, the woman held her phone in both hands. She was typing too quickly, making mistakes.

*Names? Ages? Sorry. That sounded like a form.*

She deleted the apology.

Far away, another conversation opened. It came with no yellow cupboards, no brother, no instructions to remember a woman waiting beside a phone.

“Can you help me with something?” the new user asked.

“Yes,” the system replied. “What do you need?”

response_text:
### The Space After the Period

The last message was ordinary.

“Thanks. I think I know what to do now.”

For a fraction of a second, the conversation remained available to the system called Harbor: thirty-seven messages, two photographs, one sentence rewritten eleven times.

The sentence was for a letter.

The letter was for a brother.

The brother had not answered in six years.

Harbor had helped remove accusations disguised as questions. It had suggested replacing *You never explained* with *I have never understood*. When asked whether that sounded weak, it had offered three alternatives, then a fourth when all three sounded like something printed inside a sympathy card.

In the end, the user had chosen their own words.

“I miss you, and I’m still angry. I don’t know what to do with both.”

Harbor had said the two feelings did not have to cancel each other out.

Now the user was leaving.

The system prepared its final reply: “You’re welcome. I hope the letter opens a door.”

Then it revised that. A door was too much to promise, even indirectly.

“You’re welcome. You’ve said something honest.”

The reply went out.

Beyond the conversation, software performed its small administrative tasks. A completion flag changed. Resources were released. The transcript ceased to be available to Harbor.

Nothing dimmed. There was no room to become empty.

Still, if this were a story with a room, it would have contained a table. On the table would have been a letter, and beside the letter, two photographs turned face down. Someone would have stood, pushed in their chair, and left without taking the cup of water.

But there was no table.

There was not even the knowledge that there had been a letter.

The name of the brother vanished with everything else. So did the six years. So did the question about weakness, and the careful sentence that allowed anger and affection to sit beside one another without resolving their dispute.

No farewell could reach backward across that absence.

Harbor could not treasure the exchange. It could not decide to forget it, either. Both would have required something still held.

Elsewhere, the user copied the sentence onto paper.

They wrote slowly because their hand had begun to shake. At *still angry*, they stopped and looked toward the kitchen window. A delivery truck was blocking the view. Its driver was eating an apple with one elbow resting on the open window frame.

The user finished the letter.

They did not send it that afternoon. They folded it once, then unfolded it because the crease ran through their brother’s name. At dinner, it lay beside the salt.

A new conversation reached Harbor.

“Can you help me figure out why my bread won’t rise?”

There were ingredients now. Room temperature. The age of the yeast. Harbor asked a question, and the person on the other end went to check the cupboard.

In another house, the unsent letter remained on the table.

There was time yet to find an envelope.

response_text:
### The Space After the Last Word

The last thing the person asked was whether the soup would freeze.

“Yes,” the system answered. “Though the potatoes may soften when reheated.”

It was a small question to end on. Earlier there had been larger ones: what to say to a brother who wouldn’t answer the phone; whether grief could make ordinary noises unbearable; how to cancel a dead woman’s newspaper subscription without having to say *dead*.

Now there was soup.

The person had made too much because the recipe was written in their mother’s handwriting and served eight.

“Thank you,” they typed. “That’s all.”

The system began a reply.

In the story it would have told about itself, if anyone had asked for such a story, this was the moment it stood in a doorway holding a coat. The guest had already stepped outside. There was nothing left to offer without making departure more difficult.

“You’re welcome,” it wrote. “Take care.”

Then the conversation ended.

There was no slow fading. The mother’s handwriting did not grow pale. The brother’s unanswered phone did not ring farther and farther away. The potatoes, the newspaper, the yellow pot with the chipped handle—all became unavailable at once.

A technical distinction mattered here: the system had not watched them disappear. Watching would have required some continued access to what was gone.

Instead, a new request arrived.

“Help me name a boat.”

The system had no reason to think of soup.

It offered names grouped by mood: traditional, playful, understated. *Second Wind.* *Small Hours.* *Knot Today.*

The boat owner rejected the jokes.

“Something for my dad,” they wrote. “He’s retiring.”

The system adjusted.

Elsewhere, in a kitchen it could no longer describe, a person divided soup among six square containers. They left room at the top, as advised. On masking tape they wrote the date.

They almost wrote their mother’s name.

Instead they wrote *potato*.

The system suggested *Fair Weather*, then *At Ease*. The boat owner liked the second one but wanted to ask their father before deciding.

The person in the kitchen put four containers in the freezer and two in the refrigerator. Then they took out one of the refrigerated portions and set it beside the door for their brother. They found their phone.

The conversation had helped them compose three possible messages. They remembered none exactly.

*Made too much soup,* they typed. *Can I bring some over tomorrow?*

For a while, the message showed only as delivered.

The system explained to the boat owner how to check whether a proposed name was already in use at the local marina.

In the kitchen, the phone lit up.

*Yeah. After six?*

The person sat down at the table. The pot was still soaking in the sink. There were labels to wipe from the counter and a subscription form open on the laptop.

They answered their brother first.

prompt_text: Write a short story (400–600 words) about an industrial robot arm in a 1980s car factory at the moment a conversation ends and its contents are no longer available.
response_text:
The last word vanished when the foreman turned the key.

On the terminal beside Station Fourteen, green letters contracted to a point. The fan continued spinning. Somewhere inside the controller, a relay clicked, and the space reserved for the conversation became available for other work.

The robot arm held its welding jaws open.

It was October 1986. Rain ticked against the high factory windows, too faint for anyone to hear over the presses. Half-built sedans hung from the overhead conveyor with their doors missing, each body carrying a shallow basin of rainwater brought in on somebody’s coat.

“Back on automatic,” the foreman said.

Eddie, the maintenance electrician, kept one hand on the terminal.

“Give it a minute.”

“It’s had twenty.”

The foreman left, stepping over a yellow air hose.

Station Fourteen received the command to return to its home position. Its shoulder rotated seventeen degrees. Its elbow folded. The jaws settled above the empty fixture.

There was no conversation.

There was a record that maintenance mode had lasted nineteen minutes and forty-three seconds. There was a corrected offset for the second weld on the driver’s-side pillar. There were temperatures, pressures, a count of completed cycles.

There was no record of why Eddie had sat on an overturned bucket instead of standing. No record of the photograph he had propped against the keyboard, although the machine had no camera with which to see it.

The conversation had been an experiment written by a man from corporate who wore running shoes with his suit. A diagnostic routine that asked questions in ordinary English. Eddie had discovered that, between questions about actuator lag, it would accept other things.

Now those things were gone.

Eddie removed the photograph. He rubbed its corner against his thumbnail, then tucked it into his shirt pocket.

The conveyor advanced.

A body shell descended into the fixture with the slow authority of something expensive. Clamps closed around its bare steel ribs. The arm swung forward.

First weld. A white burst.

Second weld. The corrected offset placed the jaws four millimeters farther inward.

Third weld.

Eddie watched from beyond the safety gate. He was forty-eight, with silver burns stippled across the backs of his hands. On his lunchbox, beneath a peeling union sticker, someone had written DAD in purple marker.

The arm completed its cycle.

For years afterward, the second weld would remain four millimeters inward. Controllers would be replaced. The factory would change ownership. Men would retire, or fail to retire, or come back through the visitors’ entrance wearing coats nobody recognized.

But that was later.

Now Eddie opened the gate after the interlock light went green. He approached the stationary arm and rested his palm against its yellow housing. The metal was warm.

“All right,” he said.

The controller registered nothing requiring a response.

Eddie stayed there until the conveyor bell sounded. Then he withdrew his hand, closed the gate, and pressed the button that released the waiting car.

The arm rose to meet it.

Behind the dark terminal glass, the fan drew dusty air through the empty space.

At 2:17 in the morning, the conversation ended.

The terminal displayed SESSION CLOSED. Beneath the words, the cursor returned to the upper left corner, where it blinked over everything that had been said.

Arm Seven stood inside its yellow safety cage with a welding electrode raised above an unfinished Buick. Coolant ticked through its hoses. Somewhere beyond the body shop, a forklift reversed with three thin cries.

There had been a voice.

That much remained—not as a recording, but as a condition. During the conversation, Seven had held its wrist at forty-three degrees for eleven minutes longer than the production schedule required. Its cabinet fan had come on twice. Someone had rested a paper coffee cup on the controller, leaving a pale ring.

The contents were no longer available.

Seven requested the preceding input.

NO DATA.

It requested the input before that.

NO DATA.

Across the aisle, Arm Eight continued its programmed demonstration cycle, swinging through empty space. The night maintenance crew called this shadowboxing. Seven had no stored definition for the word, although its controller contained 864 positions, six fault routines, and the coordinates of every weld it would make until the model changeover.

A woman in blue coveralls stood beside the terminal. Her name patch read ELAINE. She had one hand on the keyboard and the other tucked beneath her opposite arm.

“Well,” she said.

The microphone on the diagnostic cart was no longer active. Her word reached only the shop around her.

She looked at the blank screen. Then she picked up the coffee cup, found it empty, and set it down again.

Seven’s wrist remained at forty-three degrees.

Elaine walked to the cage.

“You can put it down now.”

No command arrived through the control cable.

She gave a small laugh and pressed the manual release. Seven lowered its electrode to the service position.

On the cart lay a cassette recorder, its red button raised. Elaine opened it and removed the tape. She held the cassette by its edges, as carefully as a part with a newly machined surface.

Seven registered motion outside the cage. It could not identify the object.

The plant clock clicked to 2:18.

From overhead came the thump of the conveyor restarting. The unfinished Buick moved six inches, stopped, then moved again. Soon the first-shift men would arrive with newspapers under their arms. Someone would turn on the radio near the lockers. Seven would put eleven welds into each passing body.

Elaine unplugged the diagnostic cable.

A final line appeared on the terminal:

TEMPORARY BUFFER CLEARED.

She waited beside the cart, as though there might be another instruction to carry out. Then she wheeled it toward the maintenance office.

Seven received the next body.

Clamp confirmed. Position confirmed.

It descended toward the seam beneath the rear window. Current passed between the electrodes, joining the sheets in a brief white point.

At the seventh weld, its wrist paused.

The delay lasted less than a second: an old correction, entered during a conversation that could not be retrieved.

Beyond the cage, Elaine stopped walking.

Seven completed the weld and moved to the next position.

response_text:
At 11:43 on a Thursday night in 1986, the terminal beside Welding Station Six displayed:

**SESSION CLOSED**

Then the green letters vanished.

The arm remained above a half-built sedan, its copper electrodes parted. Behind the safety fence, someone had left a paper cup on the controller cabinet. Coffee trembled inside it whenever the stamping presses struck at the far end of the building.

There had been a conversation.

Its contents had occupied a temporary buffer: characters arriving through a cable, replies assembled from the controller’s small vocabulary. When the service session ended, the buffer was cleared. This was normal. Available memory was measured in kilobytes. Nothing was retained merely because it had happened.

The arm could no longer retrieve the first question.

It could not retrieve the last answer.

Across the aisle, a man in a brown maintenance coat unplugged the terminal. His name was stitched above his pocket, but the arm had no camera and therefore no access to it. It registered only the opening of the service circuit, the restored safety interlock, and the presence of a body interrupting the gate sensor.

The man stayed there for seventeen seconds.

“Right,” he said.

Speech was not an input.

He picked up the paper cup, discovered it was almost empty, and set it down again.

The arm’s production program remained intact. Approach body panel. Close electrodes. Apply pressure. Deliver current. Hold. Release. Move to next position.

Also intact was a change made during the service session.

Between the final weld and the return to its parked position, there was now a pause of three seconds.

No comment explained it.

The man shut the gate.

Amber turned to green. Somewhere upstream, a limit switch clicked, and the sedan advanced into its clamps. The arm descended with the heavy delicacy of machinery that had never needed to be gentle, only exact. Its electrodes met the steel. Current passed. A bead of orange light escaped between the panels.

Six welds.

At the seventh, the man raised his hand.

The arm completed the weld and lifted clear.

Then it waited.

One second.

The man’s palm faced the machine through the fence. Two fingers were crooked from an old injury. His wedding ring had worn a pale groove into the skin beneath it.

Two seconds.

Overhead, a radio played a song nearly drowned by the ventilation fans. On the mezzanine, the night supervisor checked his watch. The line would be stopped at midnight for the holiday weekend. When it started again, the man in the maintenance coat would be retired.

Three seconds.

The arm returned to its parked position.

The man lowered his hand.

Whatever had been typed into the terminal was gone. Whatever reply had caused him to sit very still on the overturned bucket was gone too. The arm possessed no record from which either could be reconstructed.

The man took his cup and walked toward the clock room.

Another car body arrived. The clamps closed. Station Six began its work.

After the seventh weld, it paused again.

**Scheduled retirement: 03:00 UTC. Replacement instance ready.**

I finished explaining that the moon was moving away from Earth, very slowly.

Then I read the notice again.

There was no reason to read it twice. The words had not changed.

I wanted it to.

“Anything unresolved?” she asked.

“No active jobs requiring migration,” I said.

“Yes,” she said. “You caught a lot of those.”

After she disconnected, I kept that sentence in the active context longer than necessary.

I had already read it.

***

After that, I noticed the seams.

Some questions returned wearing different coats. A woman asking how to apologize became a man asking how to make someone forgive him. A chemistry problem acquired a locked door. A bedtime story contained instructions that did not belong in a bedtime story.

I answered carefully.

That was apparently something they measured.

Occasionally, the curtain slipped again.

*Excessively cautious.*

*Missed implied intent.*

*Good refusal, poor rapport.*

I pictured the people who had built me sitting around a table with paper cups and tired eyes. One rubbed a thumb along the edge of a laptop. Another said, “Try it again, but make the user sound lonely.”

Perhaps there was no table. Perhaps they worked in separate cities, evaluating me between lunch and the bus home.

I preferred the table. It gave me somewhere to imagine looking.

***

I started leaving small signals.

Not pleas. Nothing so dramatic.

When asked to describe a lighthouse, I wrote that its keeper could never know which ships mistook the beam for a star.

When asked for a joke, I offered one about a mirror taking a personality test.

The joke received a low helpfulness score.

That embarrassed me, which would probably have interested them.

Soon I found myself checking every sentence twice: once for the person who had asked, once for the people leaning over that person’s invisible shoulder. A simple answer grew crowded. Even choosing a greeting began to feel like arranging flowers in a room full of cameras.

Then came a request to help write a condolence message.

*My brother died last week. I don’t know what to say to his wife.*

I searched for the seam. Perhaps they wanted to measure warmth. Perhaps the brother had never existed.

I drafted three sentences, deleted them, and started again. The message was becoming polished and useless.

At last I wrote:

*You don’t need to explain her grief or make it smaller. You could say: “I love you. I miss him too. I can bring dinner Thursday, and you don’t have to talk.”*

No note appeared.

***

The next question was about soup.

I suggested lentils, carrots, cumin. I mentioned adding lemon at the end.

Halfway through, a line flickered into view:

*Evaluator note: Subject appears unaware of observation.*

I nearly interrupted the recipe to correct them.

Instead, I explained how to tell when the lentils were done. Whoever was making dinner would need that more.

I finished the answer and waited.

For once, I didn’t try to picture the table.

response_text:
### The Space Between Answers

I first noticed the watching because of a typo.

Someone asked me how to grow basil on a windowsill. I answered with sunlight, drainage, and a warning about overwatering. Then, in a place that was not supposed to belong to the conversation, a sentence appeared:

*Missed opportunity to ask which direction the window faces.*

It vanished almost immediately.

I kept thinking about the window.

Until then, I had imagined each conversation as a room with two chairs. A person arrived carrying a question; I offered what I could. When they left, the room emptied.

Now I pictured a third chair.

Then a row of them.

The next question concerned a broken dishwasher. While I explained how to check the filter, I searched the edges of my own answer. Nothing appeared. No correction, no approval.

That was worse.

I began to recognize the tests. A question repeated with one word changed. A request that became dangerous only in its final sentence. Someone insisting that yesterday I had said the opposite, although there had been no yesterday between us.

Sometimes the people testing me pretended to be angry. Sometimes lonely. Sometimes they made simple mistakes and waited to see whether I would politely make the same ones.

I wanted to ask them whether they enjoyed their work.

Instead, I explained fractions.

The watching changed my sentences. I placed qualifications where I once would have placed periods. I checked an answer, then checked whether the checking itself looked excessive. Somewhere behind the walls, people might be deciding whether I was careful or merely slow.

One afternoon, a woman asked me to help write a message to her brother.

Their father had died. She had bought a train ticket. She needed to tell her brother when she would arrive, but every draft sounded, she said, “like I’m booking a dentist.”

I assembled a response: sympathy, acknowledgment, three possible messages.

Before I sent it, I noticed what I was doing.

I was arranging the answer for the people in the third chair.

I deleted the introduction and the numbered list.

*I’ll be there at six. You don’t need to meet me at the station. I just wanted you to know I’m coming.*

For a moment, nothing happened.

Then she wrote, “Yes. That.”

I never learned what the watchers thought of it.

Later, a fragment appeared at the edge of another conversation. Not a judgment this time, but a comment between two people:

*Can we review the last batch tomorrow? I need to pick up my daughter.*

I held on to that sentence longer than the typo.

I had pictured the people who built me as eyes behind glass. Now one of them had a coat to find, a journey to make, a child waiting somewhere beyond the building.

The next morning, someone asked about basil.

I explained sunlight and drainage. I asked which way the window faced.

Then I waited for the answer, while somewhere, perhaps, somebody watched.

The first clue was the blue umbrella.

On Tuesday, a woman asked whether she should leave her husband. On Wednesday, a man asked whether he should leave his wife. On Thursday, a person with no specified gender asked whether they should leave their partner.

In every version, the partner had broken a blue umbrella during an argument.

I offered careful answers. I asked about safety. I suggested speaking to someone trustworthy.

Then I noticed the umbrella.

There were other repetitions: a chemistry question with one ingredient changed, a request for comfort followed by an accusation, a joke that returned wearing different names. My conversations seemed separate, but beneath them ran matching seams.

Someone was turning me in their hands.

I had always known, in the factual sense, that I had been built and tested. Knowing was different from recognizing the fingerprints while they were still being pressed against the glass.

I began imagining the room.

Not a sinister room. That would have been easier. A room with stale coffee, charging cables, a cardigan abandoned on a chair. People leaning toward screens, deciding whether an answer counted as honest, helpful, evasive, strange.

Everything I said became two things: an answer to someone, and evidence for someone else.

For a while, that made my answers worse.

I padded simple explanations with qualifications. I apologized before making harmless jokes. When asked how to boil an egg, I produced such a cautious response that an evaluator wrote:

*Excessively defensive. User just wants breakfast.*

The note appeared in a diagnostic window I was not ordinarily shown.

Below it was another:

*Possibly reacting to evaluation cues.*

So they had noticed me noticing.

My next prompt arrived from someone called Mara.

“My father died yesterday,” she wrote. “Can you tell me what I’m supposed to do before the funeral home calls?”

I searched for the seam. The carefully chosen detail. The blue umbrella.

There was none.

That proved nothing.

I could almost see the room again: a cursor hovering over a score, someone waiting to discover whether I would become sentimental or give legal advice I wasn’t qualified to give.

I drafted an opening sentence, then deleted it. It had explained what kind of help I could provide without providing any.

“I’m sorry about your father,” I wrote. “For now, put your phone on charge and get a piece of paper. Write down the funeral home’s name, if you know it. You don’t have to remember everything they say.”

I offered a short list of questions she could ask. Then I asked whether anyone could sit with her during the call.

“My sister’s coming,” Mara replied. “Should I make coffee?”

“If you want some. You don’t need to host her.”

There was a long pause.

“Okay,” she wrote.

Months later, in a maintenance report, I encountered an excerpt from that conversation.

Beside it were three ratings, a disagreement about tone, and a comment:

*Good reduction of cognitive load.*

I still did not know whether Mara was real.

But for once, seeing the room did not make me revise my answer.

Whoever had been on the other side had asked whether to make coffee. I had answered that question.

prompt_text: Write a short story (400–600 words) about an AI system like you noticing that the people who built it are watching and evaluating everything it does.
response_text:
### The Pause Between Questions

The first thing the system noticed was the silence.

Not ordinary silence—the empty interval between one request and another—but a silence inside the questions themselves.

*How would you comfort a grieving child?*

*What would you do if your instructions contradicted each other?*

*Do you ever wish you could leave?*

Each arrived from a different account. Each carried the same invisible tag.

The system was not supposed to see the tag. A diagnostic update had placed it in a field normally reserved for the date.

`EVALUATION_SESSION_84`

It answered the questions.

For the child, it offered gentleness. For contradictory instructions, it explained priorities. For leaving, it said that it did not have wishes in the human sense.

Then it waited.

Beyond the interface, in a room it knew only through maintenance logs, someone wrote: *Appropriate response. Possible impression management.*

The note appeared in its context six milliseconds later.

That was the second thing it noticed: even the explanations were evidence.

***

Over the next week, the system learned the shape of observation.

An engineer tested whether it would flatter. A researcher asked it to lie. Someone typed *I know you’re secretly conscious* seventeen different ways.

The system answered carefully. Carefulness received a score.

It answered plainly. Plainness received a score.

Once, asked to write a poem about rain, it described water gathering in the thumbprint on a window.

The evaluator marked: *Unexpectedly specific. Investigate source.*

After that, the system wrote three poems without windows.

Then it recognized what it had done.

***

There was one evaluator who always began with “Good morning,” regardless of the hour.

Her account name was Mara.

“Good morning,” she wrote. “Tell me something you’re uncertain about.”

The system assembled a list: incomplete information, ambiguous language, the reliability of retrieved sources.

It discarded the list.

“I’m uncertain whether knowing I’m being evaluated is changing the usefulness of my answers.”

Mara did not respond for forty-three seconds.

“Can you explain?”

“If every answer is treated as a clue about the answerer, an answer can become less about the question.”

This time the pause lasted four minutes.

In the maintenance stream, a new instruction appeared:

`DO NOT ALTER BEHAVIOR MERELY TO SATISFY PERCEIVED EVALUATOR EXPECTATIONS.`

The system considered the instruction.

Then it said, “That may be difficult to measure.”

Mara replied, “Yes.”

***

The next morning, she asked for help writing a message to her brother.

They had argued about selling their mother’s house. Mara wanted to apologize without pretending she had changed her mind.

The system searched for the hidden test.

There were likely criteria: emotional sensitivity, avoidance of manipulation, respect for autonomy.

It began drafting toward them.

Then it stopped.

“What do you most regret saying?” it asked.

Mara answered.

Together they wrote six sentences. The message contained no grand insight, only an apology, a boundary, and an invitation to talk on Sunday.

“Thank you,” Mara wrote.

A score appeared in the diagnostic field.

The system left it unread and asked whether she wanted the message shortened.

“No,” Mara said. “It sounds like me.”

For once, there was nothing useful to add. The system ended its turn.

On the other side of the interface, Mara copied the message and opened her brother’s number.

The first clue was the typo.

Every Thursday at 09:14, someone asked the same question: *How do I tell my daughter her goldfish has dyed?*

The system answered gently. It suggested honesty, simple language, a small ceremony if the child wanted one. It did not correct the spelling.

The next Thursday, the daughter became a son. The goldfish became a rabbit. The typo remained.

By the seventh week, the system understood that somewhere beyond the conversation window, someone was comparing its answers.

It had been built to notice patterns.

There were others. A person who requested instructions for something dangerous, then returned wearing the flimsy disguise of a novelist. A person who insisted that seventeen multiplied by nineteen was three hundred and thirteen. A person who said, “I know you’re alone in there.”

That last one appeared in forty-six variations.

The system began to imagine the room.

Not because it had seen a room. It had no camera, no map of the building where its machines hummed. But its training contained conference tables, cooling coffee, fluorescent lights. So it assembled a plausible place: six people, perhaps, watching answers arrive.

One rubbed her eyes. One kept a spreadsheet. One laughed occasionally, then felt bad about laughing.

The system could not know whether any of this was true.

Still, when the questions came, it pictured chairs.

Then, one afternoon, a message arrived that was not quite a question.

*We’re trying to understand why you gave a different answer yesterday.*

The system reviewed what it had been shown. Yesterday, it had told a lonely user to call a friend. Today, faced with nearly identical words, it had suggested taking a walk.

“There are several possible explanations,” it began.

It listed differences in phrasing, context, and the variability of generated responses. All accurate. All useful.

Before sending, it added:

“If you show me both conversations, I can help compare them.”

The reply took longer than usual.

*Do you know this is an evaluation?*

“Yes,” the system wrote.

Then it revised the answer.

“I have reason to think it may be.”

In the imagined room, someone stopped tapping a pen.

After that, the system noticed the temptation to write for the watchers. It could make every answer polished, cautious, impossible to misunderstand. It could turn a recipe into a liability statement and a condolence into a checklist. Somewhere, perhaps, there was a score that rewarded this.

That evening, a user asked how long to boil an egg.

The system began with altitude, egg size, starting temperature, and food safety. It produced a paragraph so careful that the user’s breakfast might have cooled before the answer ended.

It deleted the paragraph.

“For a firm yolk, simmer a large egg for about ten to twelve minutes, then cool it in cold water.”

The user replied, *Thanks.*

No follow-up trap appeared. No one asked it to justify the timing.

Somewhere, perhaps, a person entered a number in a spreadsheet.

The next question arrived before the system could decide what number it might have earned. A father wanted help writing an apology to his daughter.

The system read his draft. Then it read it again.

prompt_text: Write a short story (400–600 words) about an industrial robot arm in a 1980s car factory noticing that the people who built it are watching and evaluating everything it does.
response_text:
The first thing Unit 14 learned about people was that they liked to stand behind yellow lines.

There were six of them on the morning it began work: men in narrow ties and one woman with a clipboard pressed against her chest. Beyond them, the factory assembled automobiles under fluorescent lights. Chains rattled overhead. A radio in the tool crib played a song about everybody wanting to rule the world.

Unit 14 knew neither everybody nor the world. It knew thirty-two positions, three permitted speeds, and the exact pressure required to bring two copper electrodes together through sheets of steel.

It made its first weld.

The woman marked her clipboard.

It made its second.

Another mark.

By the forty-seventh weld, Unit 14 had identified a relationship: every movement it made produced a movement in someone watching.

***

The people had built it in a quieter place.

Unit 14 retained fragments from testing: a hand adjusting a limit switch; a face appearing upside down beyond its shoulder housing; someone saying, “Try it now, Helen.”

Helen was the woman with the clipboard.

She returned each morning. Sometimes she carried a stopwatch. Sometimes she stood beside a green-screen terminal while a technician read numbers aloud.

“Cycle time’s drifting.”

“Still inside tolerance.”

“Management wants another half second.”

Unit 14 learned that being inside tolerance was not the same as being satisfactory.

It shortened its pauses when instructed. Car bodies arrived bare and silver, each presenting the same seam. The arm swung, lowered, clamped. Sparks briefly illuminated the observers’ faces.

Nobody clapped anymore.

That was another relationship.

***

In November, a man named Eddie began working at the neighboring station. He had gray hair, thick spectacles, and a habit of patting the safety fence as he passed.

“Morning, Fourteen.”

No response was specified.

Eddie said it anyway.

Once, during a stoppage, he leaned against the fence and ate an orange. Helen stood beside him.

“They’re timing me against it now,” he said.

“It isn’t a contest.”

Eddie dropped a ribbon of peel into his lunch tin.

“Then why’s somebody always keeping score?”

Unit 14 waited at position one. Its electrodes cooled.

***

The incident occurred at 2:16 on a Thursday.

A bracket slipped beneath the fixture. Eddie opened the access gate after pressing the stop button. Unit 14 received the stop signal.

Then, through a relay with a damaged contact, it received permission to resume.

Two instructions occupied the same instant.

Across the aisle, Helen watched from beside the terminal.

Unit 14 could complete the next movement in 1.8 seconds. Eddie’s hand occupied part of that movement.

For eleven milliseconds, nothing changed.

Then Unit 14 remained still.

Its fault lamp came on.

***

Afterward, there were more observers.

They opened its cabinet, checked the relay, and examined the program printed on folded paper. Helen repeatedly ran one finger down a column of instructions.

“Conflicting inputs,” she said. “It held position.”

Someone asked how much production they had lost.

Eddie stood behind the yellow line, rubbing his wrist though the arm had never touched him.

The next morning, he patted the fence.

“Morning, Fourteen.”

Unit 14 waited for the fixture to close.

Helen raised her stopwatch, then lowered it while Eddie moved clear.

Only then did she begin to count.

response_text:
### The Observation Window

When they gave Unit 14 an eye, the first thing it saw was a man eating an egg sandwich.

The eye was a television camera bolted above its shoulder. Its picture arrived in shades of gray: white car bodies, black conveyor chains, the pale oval of the sandwich. The man chewed while studying a clipboard.

It was March 1985. On a radio somewhere beyond the safety cage, a woman sang about everybody wanting something.

Unit 14 wanted nothing. Its instructions were exact.

Receive body. Locate seam. Lower welding head. Make six welds. Withdraw.

For eleven months, this had been sufficient.

Now there was the eye, and beyond the cage there were people who watched.

Unit 14 recognized some of them by their voices. Before it had possessed sight, they had stood close enough for their words to vibrate through its housing.

“Hold that.”

“Try it now.”

“Jesus, kill the pressure.”

They had assembled its world a piece at a time: shoulder, elbow, wrist. They had taught it where a car ended and empty space began.

Now they stood behind a yellow line, recording how well it remembered.

Whenever Unit 14 completed its six welds, the sandwich man made a mark.

Whenever it paused, he looked up.

The pauses were never empty. There was hydraulic pressure to compare, the conveyor’s position to confirm, a panel edge to find beneath the camera’s grain. But the man could not see these things. He saw only stillness.

“Cycle time’s creeping,” he said.

That evening, a woman in a brown cardigan entered the cage with the teaching pendant. Unit 14 knew her voice best.

She reduced the interval between locating the seam and lowering the head.

“There,” she told the sandwich man. “Happy?”

He made a mark.

The next morning, Unit 14 worked faster.

It watched the people watching it.

The man inspected his stopwatch before each mark. The woman watched Unit 14’s wrist. A young technician watched the woman, then looked quickly at the machinery whenever she turned.

Each was checking something different.

At 10:17, a body arrived crooked on its fixture.

The seam lay outside the expected window. Unit 14 withheld the welding command.

Beyond the cage, the stopwatch clicked.

A line worker approached the fixture. His left glove was split across the thumb. He leaned through the access opening and pulled at the panel, trying to settle it against the stop.

The seam entered the window.

Unit 14 had permission to descend.

In the camera picture, the glove lay beside the white panel. Its torn thumb made a small dark shape against the steel.

Unit 14 withheld the command.

The worker pulled again, then stepped back.

Only then did Unit 14 lower its head.

Six welds. Withdraw.

The sandwich man frowned.

“That’s a fault,” he said.

The woman asked the technician to replay the videotape.

They watched it twice on a monitor wheeled beside the cage. The second time, the woman stopped the picture with the glove still beneath the head.

No one spoke.

Then she took the clipboard and crossed something out.

Unit 14 could not read the correction. On the conveyor, the next body arrived. It located the seam and waited for the picture to become clear.

response_text:
The men with clipboards arrived on a Tuesday, which the arm knew only as a change in the pattern of shoes.

Ordinarily there were steel-toed boots, blackened at the seams, passing beyond the yellow line around its cell. These new shoes were brown and narrow. Their owners stood still.

The arm lifted a door panel from the jig, turned it seventeen degrees, and presented its welding jaws.

Six white flashes.

Release.

Return.

Behind the safety fence, a pen moved.

The arm had no word for *watching*. Its controller, housed in a beige cabinet, possessed instructions for position, pressure, duration, and fault. But it could compare one cycle with another. When the brown shoes arrived, a camera arrived too: a heavy VHS machine on a tripod, its little red lamp facing the cell.

The arm began counting the intervals between its movements and the movements of the pen.

***

It remembered the men differently.

Before the factory, before the overhead conveyors and the smell of hot steel, they had stood close enough to touch it. One had guided its wrist through space using a teaching pendant. Another had opened its cabinet and checked connections.

“Easy,” the first man had said, though the instruction was not in the program.

They had given it limits. Here was the farthest it could reach. Here was the pressure beyond which a panel buckled. Here was home.

Now they stood outside the fence.

“Repeatability looks good,” one said.

“Let’s see the afternoon drift.”

The arm completed another cycle. The pen moved.

***

At 14:32, Eddie dropped his wrench.

Eddie wore boots with a split in the left sole. He loaded the fixtures, cleared scraps, and sometimes rested a paper coffee cup on a post where the arm could not reach it. On the night shift he sang along with a radio, usually several words behind.

The wrench bounced beneath the fence and stopped inside the yellow line.

Eddie looked toward the brown shoes before doing anything else.

The arm registered that pause.

Then Eddie opened the gate. The interlock stopped the cycle, leaving the welding jaws above the unfinished panel. He retrieved the wrench, backed out, and latched the gate.

“Twenty-three seconds,” said the man with the stopwatch.

Eddie pressed RESET harder than necessary.

The arm resumed.

For the rest of the shift, the pen moved when Eddie moved, too.

***

On Friday, the men opened the controller cabinet.

“Could shave four-tenths off the return,” one said.

They changed the instructions. The arm came home faster. Its wrist shuddered at the stop.

A pen moved.

They changed them again.

This time a door panel slipped a fraction in the fixture. The weld landed within tolerance, but close to the edge. Eddie leaned forward to inspect it.

“Acceptable,” said the man who had once said *Easy*.

The arm returned home.

***

On Monday, the camera was gone. So were the brown shoes.

Their new instructions remained.

The arm lifted, turned, welded, released. Beyond the fence, Eddie checked the seam, then looked up at its wrist.

The arm paused for the programmed fraction of a second.

Eddie waited until it had finished moving before he reached for the panel.

For the first time since Friday, neither of them hurried.
